monomeric U(VI) can be reduced to monomeric U (IV) by microbes or iron minerals in uranium-contaminated environments, and that the U(IV) species can be re-oxidized to U(VI) during X-ray microprobe analysis.

the oxidation of uranium(IV) by X-ray microbeams.
the chemical speciation of uranium in the environment.
the chemical speciation of U(IV), U(V) and U(VI) in environmental samples and how the speciation is affected by the oxidation of U(IV).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the oxidation state and speciation of uranium can be determined by microbeam X-ray absorption spectroscopies but the oxidation state of U(IV)-containing species can be affected by X-ray beam-induced oxidation.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the oxidation of monomerc U(IV) species by the microbeam is a function of the beam intensity and the sample composition.
the oxidation state of uranium in environmental systems is highly dependent on the sample preparation, the experimental setup and the analysis technique.
XAS analysis of U(VI), U(IV) and U(III) species at microbeam size is possible but requires careful consideration of the sample preparation, beam exposure and data reduction procedures.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of microbeam analysis of U-containing samples may lead to the overestimation of U(IV), which is a critical component in the biogeochemistry of uranium.
the oxidation state of uranium is not necessarily conserved during microbeam analysis, even when using a low-energy X-ray beam.
beam-induced reoxidation of monomeric uranium is a concern for microbeam analysis of uranium-containing environmental samples.
